question: Which immigration programs are managed through Express Entry?
answer:
The immigration programs managed through Express Entry are:

- Canadian Experience Class
- Federal Skilled Worker Program
- Federal Skilled Trades Program

(Source: Immigrate through Express Entry, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry.html)

question: How much Canadian work experience do I need to qualify for the Canadian Experience Class?
answer: To qualify for the Canadian Experience Class, you need at least 1 year (or 1,560 hours) of skilled work experience in Canada within the 3 years before you apply. This can be a combination of full-time or part-time work in 1 or more jobs. The work must be in a TEER category 0, 1, 2, or 3 job, and you must have been authorized to work in Canada during this time. (Source: Express Entry: Canadian Experience Class, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply/canadian-experience-class.html)

question: What minimum language level does the Federal Skilled Worker Program require?
answer: The Federal Skilled Worker Program requires a minimum Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) level of 7 in each of the four language abilities (speaking, listening, reading, and writing) for the first official language. For the second official language, you can get additional points if you have a score of at least CLB 5 in each of the four abilities. (Source: Express Entry: Federal Skilled Worker Program, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply/federal-skilled-workers.html)

question: Do I need proof of funds if I'm applying under the Canadian Experience Class?
answer: No, you don't need to show proof of funds if you're applying under the Canadian Experience Class. (Source: Documents for Express Entry: Proof of funds, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/proof-funds.html)

facts_supported: applying under the Canadian Experience Class

question: Can I use the equity in my house or money borrowed from a friend as proof of funds for Express Entry?
answer: No, you cannot use equity in your house or money borrowed from a friend as proof of funds for Express Entry. You must have legal access to the funds and cannot borrow the money from another person. (Source: Documents for Express Entry: Proof of funds, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/proof-funds.html)

facts_supported: can't use equity on real property
can't borrow this money from another person

question: Does work I did while studying full-time in Canada count toward the Canadian Experience Class?
answer: No, you can't count work experience if you were studying full-time while you worked (Source: Express Entry: Canadian Experience Class, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply/canadian-experience-class.html).

question: Is a job offer required for the Federal Skilled Trades Program?
answer: A job offer is not strictly required for the Federal Skilled Trades Program. You can qualify with either a valid job offer or a certificate of qualification in your skilled trade issued by a Canadian provincial, territorial or federal authority (Source: Express Entry: Federal Skilled Trades Program, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply/federal-skilled-trades.html).

question: How much is the fee for a Canadian study permit?
answer: The fee for a Canadian study permit is $150 CAD. (Source: Study permit, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit.html)

question: How much money do I need for living expenses as a single student if I apply for a study permit on or after September 1, 2026, outside Quebec?
answer: If you apply for a study permit on or after September 1, 2026, outside Quebec, you will need $23,448 for living expenses as a single student. (Source: Study permit: Get the right documents - Proof of financial support, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/get-documents/financial-support.html)

question: If I applied for a study permit in 2025 and bring 2 family members to Ontario, how much do we need for living expenses for the first year?
answer: For a study permit application in 2025, if you are bringing 2 family members to Ontario, you will need $35,040 for living expenses for the first year. (Source: Study permit: Get the right documents - Proof of financial support, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/get-documents/financial-support.html)

question: How many hours per week can an international student work off campus during the school term?
answer: During regular school terms or semesters, an international student can work up to 24 hours per week off campus. (Source: Work off campus as an international student, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/work-off-campus.html)

question: Can international students work more hours off campus during summer or winter break?
answer: Yes, during scheduled breaks in the school year, such as summer and winter holidays, international students can work unlimited hours off campus. (Source: Work off campus as an international student, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/work-off-campus.html)

question: Can I work off campus if I'm only enrolled in an English as a second language program?
answer: No, you can't work off campus without a work permit if you're only enrolled in an English as a second language (ESL) program. (Source: Work off campus as an international student, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/work-off-campus.html)

facts_supported: only enrolled in an English or French as a second language (ESL/FSL) program

question: What are the eligibility requirements to get a study permit?
answer:
To be eligible for a study permit, you must:

- be enrolled at a designated learning institution (DLI)
- prove you have enough money to pay for your tuition fees, living expenses for yourself and any family members who come with you to Canada, and return transportation for yourself and any family members who come with you to Canada
- obey the law, have no criminal record and get a police certificate (if required)
- be in good health and get a medical exam (if required)
- prove to an officer that you will leave Canada when your study permit expires

(Source: Study permit: Who can apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/eligibility.html)

facts_supported: enough money to pay for your tuition fees
leave Canada when your study permit expires

question: How long after finishing my program do I have to apply for a post-graduation work permit?
answer: You have 180 days from the date of your program completion to apply for a post-graduation work permit. (Source: Post-graduation work permit: Who can apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html)

facts_supported: within 180 days of confirmation that you completed your program

question: What is the minimum length of a study program for PGWP eligibility?
answer: The minimum length of a study program for PGWP eligibility is 8 months (or 900 hours for Quebec credentials) (Source: Post-graduation work permit: About the post-graduation work permit (PGWP), https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/about.html).

question: What language test level do I need for a PGWP if I graduated with a bachelor's degree?
answer:
If you submitted your PGWP application before November 1, 2024, you don’t need to meet the language requirement for your program. (Source: Post-graduation work permit: Who can apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html)

If you apply on or after November 1, 2024, you must prove your English or French language skills with a minimum level of Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB) 7 in English or Niveaux de competence linguistique canadiens (NCLC) 7 in French in all 4 language areas. (Source: Post-graduation work permit: Who can apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html)

question: What language level is required for a PGWP after a college diploma program?
answer: The language level required for a PGWP after a college diploma program is a minimum of Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB) 7 in English or Niveaux de competence linguistique canadiens (NCLC) 7 in French in all 4 language areas (reading, writing, listening, speaking). (Source: Post-graduation work permit: Who can apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html)

question: Can I get a second post-graduation work permit after completing another program?

question: My master's program was only 1 year long. Can I still get a 3-year PGWP?
answer: As of February 15, 2024, you can apply for a 3-year PGWP even if your master’s program was less than 2 years, as long as your program was at least 8 months and you meet all other eligibility requirements. (Source: Post-graduation work permit: About the post-graduation work permit (PGWP), https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/about.html)

question: What is the fee to apply for a post-graduation work permit?
answer: The fee to apply for a post-graduation work permit is $255 (Source: Post-graduation work permit: How to apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/apply.html).

question: My study permit expired before I applied for my PGWP. What can I do?
answer: If your study permit expired before you applied for your Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP), you need to apply to restore your status as a student to be eligible to apply for your PGWP. You must pay additional fees to restore your status. Because of system limitations, you must pay the fees to restore your status as a student online and attach a copy of the receipt to your PGWP online application. You don’t need to make a separate application to restore your status as a student (Source: Post-graduation work permit: How to apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/apply.html).

facts_supported: restore your status as a student

question: What is the difference between an open work permit and an employer-specific work permit?
answer:
The main differences between an open work permit and an employer-specific work permit are:

1. **Employer-specific work permit**:
   - Lets you work in Canada under specific conditions, including the employer, location, and occupation (Source: Employer-specific work permits: eligibility, LMIA, and application steps, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/employer-specific.html).

2. **Open work permit**:
   - Lets you work for any employer in Canada, except those on the non-compliant list or those regularly offering specific adult services (Source: Open work permits: eligibility, restrictions, and application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/open-work-permit.html).
   - You don’t need a job offer to apply, and the employer doesn’t need to apply for a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) or pay the employer compliance fee (Source: Open work permits: eligibility, restrictions, and application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/open-work-permit.html).

facts_supported: work for any employer in Canada

question: Do I need a job offer to apply for an open work permit?
answer: No, you don't need a job offer to apply for an open work permit. (Source: Open work permits: eligibility, restrictions, and application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/open-work-permit.html)

facts_supported: don't need a job offer to apply for an open work permit

question: What is an LMIA and when does my employer need one?
answer: A labour market impact assessment (LMIA) is a document that proves there’s a need to hire a foreign worker to fill the job. Most jobs need an LMIA. Your employer needs one unless the job is LMIA-exempt (Source: Employer-specific work permits: eligibility, LMIA, and application steps, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/employer-specific.html).

facts_supported: need to hire a foreign worker

question: Do business visitors need a work permit to work in Canada?
answer: No, business visitors do not need a work permit to work in Canada. (Source: Who can work in Canada without a work permit – exemptions and eligibility, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/work-without-permit.html)

question: My work permit expired. How long do I have to apply to restore my status?
answer: You must apply to restore your status no more than 90 days after your status expired. (Source: Restore your status and get a work permit, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/restore.html)

facts_supported: within 90 days of losing your status

question: Can I change employers if I have an open work permit?
answer: Yes, if you have an open work permit, you can change employers at any time while your work permit is valid. (Source: Extend or change the conditions on your work permit: Changing jobs or employers, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/extend/change-jobs-employers.html)

question: I lost the job tied to my employer-specific work permit. Can I keep working for another employer?
answer: If you lose the job connected to your employer-specific work permit and want to continue working in Canada, you must get a new job offer and apply to change the conditions on your work permit. You must stop working for this or any other employer until your new work permit is approved or you receive a work authorization email (Source: Extend or change the conditions on your work permit: Changing jobs or employers, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/extend/change-jobs-employers.html).

facts_supported: get a new job offer and apply to change the conditions

question: How long can most visitors stay in Canada?
answer: Most visitors can stay in Canada for up to 6 months. (Source: Visitor visa: About the document, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/about-visitor-visa.html)

question: How do I extend my stay in Canada as a visitor?
answer: To extend your stay in Canada as a visitor, you need to apply for a visitor record. A visitor record is not a visa. You should apply for an extension at least 30 days before the authorized end of your stay. (Source: Extend your stay in Canada (visitor record), https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/extend-stay.html)

question: How far in advance should I apply to extend my stay as a visitor?
answer: You should apply at least 30 days before your current status expires. (Source: Visitor record: Who can apply?, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/extend-stay/eligibility.html)

facts_supported: at least 30 days before your current status expires

question: How much does an electronic travel authorization (eTA) cost?

question: How long can my parents stay in Canada with a super visa?
answer:
If your parents applied for a super visa on or after June 22, 2023, they are eligible to stay for 5 years at a time. (Source: Super visa for parents and grandparents – How long you can stay in Canada, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/parent-grandparent-super-visa/length-stay-canada.html)

If they entered Canada before June 22, 2023, they can only stay for the length of time the border officer granted them when they entered Canada. (Source: Super visa for parents and grandparents – How long you can stay in Canada, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/parent-grandparent-super-visa/length-stay-canada.html)

question: What is the fee for a Canadian visitor visa?
answer: The fee for a Canadian visitor visa is $100 per individual or $500 for a family of 5 or more people. Additionally, there is a biometrics fee of $85 per individual or up to $170 for a family, if applicable. (Source: How to apply for a visitor visa, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/apply-visitor-visa.html)

question: Do US green card holders need an eTA to fly to Canada?
answer: No, lawful permanent residents of the United States, such as US green card holders, are exempt from the eTA requirement. They must show a valid passport from their country or territory of nationality and a valid green card for all methods of travel to Canada. (Source: Electronic travel authorization (eTA): Who can apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/eta/eligibility.html)

question: Who is eligible to sponsor a spouse or common-law partner to Canada?
answer:
To be eligible to sponsor a spouse or common-law partner to Canada, you must meet the following criteria:

- You must be at least 18 years old.
- You must be a Canadian citizen, a permanent resident of Canada, or a person registered in Canada as an Indian under the Canadian Indian Act.
- You must not receive social assistance for reasons other than a disability.
- You must not be in prison, bankrupt, under a removal order, or charged with a serious crime.
- You must not have sponsored another spouse, common-law partner, or conjugal partner in the past, unless that person has become a Canadian citizen or has been a permanent resident of Canada for at least five years.
- You must promise to financially support your spouse or common-law partner and their dependent children (if applicable) and provide for their basic needs, such as food, shelter, and clothing, without needing social assistance from the government.

(Source: Sponsor your spouse, partner or children: Who you can sponsor, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children/who-you-can-sponsor.html)

question: How long do I need to have been physically present in Canada to apply for citizenship?
answer: You must have been physically present in Canada for at least 1,095 days (3 years) during your 5-year eligibility period (Source: Canadian citizenship for adults and minor children: Who can apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/adult-minor/who.html).

question: Does time I spent in Canada as an international student count toward citizenship?
